paragraphs.text: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy-2 (FAME2) is an autosomal dominant disorder. Its core triad is cortical tremor, multifocal myoclonus, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures (Crompton et al., 2012). Symptoms usually begin in the second to third decade. Expressivity varies within and between families, and the frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures ranges from 15 to 100% across families (Corbett et al., 2019). Some patients also have complex partial or focal seizures. In 1 family with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME), 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation (Guerrini et al., 2001).

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree in which 8 individuals had a nonprogressive disorder beginning between the ages of 12 and 50 years. All patients had predominantly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most affected individuals rarely had seizures and had normal cognitive levels. However, 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had both frontotemporal and generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic study suggested that the myoclonus was cortical in origin. In 5 patients, EMG and EEG recorded over the contralateral rolandic area showed significant coherence at 8 to 25 Hz, with EEG activity preceding EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms. In 2 individuals there was also significant ipsilateral EEG-EMG coherence, consistent with transcallosal spread of myoclonic activity. The C-reflex at rest was enhanced, and somatosensory and visual evoked potentials were of high amplitude. Compared with controls, the resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation was significantly reduced (38%; SD +/- 7; P = 0.01). The post-motor evoked potential silent period was significantly shortened (101 ms vs 137 ms in controls). The authors concluded that these findings suggested diffuse cortical hyperexcitability, particularly involving frontotemporal circuits.

paragraphs.text: Labauge et al. (2002) described a 4-generation European kindred with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME) that included 18 members. They examined 15 living members clinically and studied 5 patients electrophysiologically. Ten living and 3 deceased relatives had the clinical characteristics of FAME. Among the 10 living patients, mean age at onset was 41 years (range, 30-60 years). Eight of the 13 affected individuals had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electrophysiologic studies confirmed the diagnosis in all 5 patients tested. The authors noted that this family extended the occurrence of FAME to non-Japanese patients.

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years) had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members. Three presymptomatic members also had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long-loop reflex I. After 1.5 years of follow-up, these 3 members developed hand tremor and myoclonus of the upper limbs.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) studied a 6-generation FAME kindred of European descent ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. All 55 affected members had fine hand tremor, typically beginning in adolescence (median age, 15 years; range, 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and began later than the hand tremor (median age, 17 years; range, 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range, 18-76 years). Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. In this family, the most common phenotype was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) described a second ADCME family from Tuscany (family B), a 4-generation kindred with 5 affected members (4 living). They also noted that the clinical features of the previously described family A closely resembled those of family B. All patients in family B had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs. Cortical tremor was the presenting symptom in all affected individuals and appeared between the ages of 18 and 50 years. All but 1 affected individual had epilepsy, characterized by rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures that were at times precipitated by visual stimuli. Two patients had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One individual had borderline cognitive level, and the others had normal intelligence. All patients had generalized or focal paroxysmal EEG activity. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflexes were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. No patient had evidence of cardiovascular disease. The 2 oldest mutation carriers developed age-related dementia. The authors noted that myoclonus often worsened at advanced age.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) studied the Tuscan family originally reported by Guerrini et al. (2001) (family A). Sequencing of genes in the ADCME critical region identified an in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG). The change replaces 5 amino acids (HGGAL) with 4 new residues (QFGR) in the third intracellular loop of the receptor. The variant cosegregated completely with the disease. It was absent from 575 unrelated controls from Tuscany and from dbSNP, the Exome Variant Server, and the 1000 Genomes Project, totaling 16,080 chromosomes. Targeted capture and next-generation sequencing of all coding regions in the critical region in 2 affected members of family A found the ADRA2B variant to be the only relevant change. The same variant was present in a second Tuscan ADCME family (family B), which shared the disease haplotype across the entire critical region. No ADRA2B mutations were found in BAFME pedigrees from southern Italy that mapped to the same locus. In transfected cells, the mutant receptor localized normally to the plasma membrane and was internalized in an arrestin-3-dependent manner. However, it did not form a stable complex with spinophilin after 10 minutes of epinephrine stimulation. In Xenopus oocytes, spinophilin increased the EC50 for epinephrine with the wildtype receptor but not with the mutant receptor. The authors concluded that the mutant receptor increased the intensity of calcium signaling, representing a gain-of-function effect.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from 2 individuals from the Australian-New Zealand family reported by Crompton et al. (2012), 1 individual from an Italian family, and 3 individuals from a French-Spanish family. Using repeat expansion detection methods, they identified expansion of an ATTTT repeat and insertion of an ATTTC repeat in the first intron of the STARD7 gene in all FAME samples tested. The ATTTC repeat was absent from whole-genome sequencing data from 69 controls. The endogenous ATTTT repeat varied in length in the normal population but was not expanded to the same extent as in patients. Using a repeat-primed PCR assay, the authors detected the expansion in 137 of 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families. Of 24 tested family members without a FAME diagnosis, 2 carried the expansion; both were from younger generations and were likely presymptomatic. Among 72 additional individuals clinically similar to FAME, the expansion was found in 20 of 20 familial cases from 6 families and in 1 of 52 singleton cases. Eight of 13 family members with an uncertain diagnosis, usually tremor alone, carried the expansion. The expansion did not amplify in any of 28 control DNA samples. In all, 158 individuals from 22 pedigrees tested positive. Long-read sequencing in 1 individual from the Australian-New Zealand family showed 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats in an SMRT read, but 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats with some interruptions in a nanopore read, suggesting somatic variation in repeat size. In an individual from another family, a nanopore read contained 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats (4,645 bp in total). The ATTTC repeat primer detected FAME with a sensitivity of 100% in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chromosome 2. These included 2 families carrying the ADRA2B variant reported by De Fusco et al. (2014), which led Corbett et al. (2019) to conclude that the ADRA2B allele is very likely not causative.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 2 Tuscan families with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy, De Fusco et al. (2014) identified an in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG). The change replaces 5 residues (HGGAL) with 4 new residues (QFGR) in the third intracellular loop (p.H225_L229delinsQ225_F_G_R228). The variant cosegregated with the disease and was absent from 16,080 control chromosomes. The mutant receptor failed to form a stable complex with spinophilin after epinephrine stimulation, and it increased epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling in Xenopus oocytes.

paragraphs.text: In affected individuals from 22 FAME2 pedigrees, Corbett et al. (2019) identified an inserted ATTTC pentanucleotide repeat accompanied by expansion of the endogenous ATTTT repeat in the first intron of the STARD7 gene. The pedigrees included an Australian-New Zealand family, Italian families, a French-Spanish family, Sephardic Jewish families, and a South African family. The variant was detected by whole-genome sequencing and repeat-primed PCR, and its structure was characterized by long-read sequencing. On the forward strand of chromosome 2, the pathogenic repeat had the structure (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n. In 1 patient, an SMRT read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats, and a nanopore read from another patient contained 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats. The expansion segregated with the disease in all 158 individuals who tested positive, including 137 of 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported families. It was absent from 69 control genomes and 28 control DNA samples. STARD7 mRNA and protein levels were not altered in patient fibroblasts.
